title: Welcome
logline: A fire alarm at three in the morning, a chastity talk with a slideshow, a beach cleanup that is absolutely not a date — and after a barn party, Lena asks to be walked home the long way.

s01.slug: FRIDAY · 3:12 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT LAWN
body: Fifty-eight minutes after *Goodnight, Jack*, Delgado Hall goes off. It’s the goose again, the same flat, outraged horn as the first time, strobes stuttering down every hallway, three hundred and ten freshmen coming down the stairwells in whatever they sleep in. Jack wasn’t asleep, which saves him a step. He goes down the east stairs in yesterday’s flannel and yesterday’s jeans, still smelling faintly of the Hobart, the RAZR shut in his pocket on a text he hasn’t deleted and isn’t going to.

Out on the lawn the fog has come in off the Lagoon to the knee, and it beads on everything wool: sweaters, blankets, one girl’s entire Snuggie. The tide is out, and the Lagoon smells like the back room of a bait shop. The eucalyptus drips. Over in the Anacapa lot the sodium lamps have gone orange in the fog, and everybody standing under them looks jaundiced.

On the lobby steps Priya stands in her Fremont High hoodie with the air horn in one hand and, held over her head in the other like a picket sign for a strike with one member, a single laminate: THE LAWN IS NOT A SOCIAL EVENT. She says nothing. She has said it all in writing.

The roll call is Kevin’s. Clipboard, navy quarter-zip zipped to the sternum over plaid pajama pants, a flag-football voice that carries without yelling. “Pruitt?” Nothing. At the far end of the building Doug Pruitt stands barefoot on the wet concrete with his pillow under his arm. “Pruitt’s here.” Kevin gets to Jack and takes him in from the sneakers up. “Costigan. Present, and fully dressed, at three in the morning.” The pen makes its check. “I don’t ask questions, bro. I just take attendance.”

Margot is off by herself at the edge of the lamplight in a black peacoat over black, visibly not cold, the Moleskine open. She doesn’t look up when he stops beside her. She writes, and tilts the page so he can read it by strobe: ALARM 2. “Eighteen days,” she says. “That’s not a schedule. That’s a person.” She clicks the pen shut and goes back to the crowd, working through it methodically, face by face, left to right.
Theo comes out among the last, barefoot in the navy silk robe, with the gray camera bag on one shoulder and the black one on the other and nothing in his hands. “No espresso machine?” “It’s insured.”
“FIREMAN.”

Laney comes across the lawn with her arms already up. She’s been home two hours from her first night as a Pi Lam, and it shows in the best way: Thursday’s pink PI LAM RODEO tee under the gray Cardinal Mooney hoodie that stopped being Jack’s at the first alarm, the hoodie to her knees, and on top of everything the pink straw cowboy hat, tipped back. “They were *lucky*, fireman,” she says, and gets him around the neck. “You *said*.” She lets go to turn a slow circle on the wet grass, one hand on the hat. “I was adored, sugar. *Professionally*.” Then she takes the hat off, sets it on Jack’s head, squares it with both thumbs and pats the crown. “Hold this.” And she’s off into the fog, yelling somebody’s name.

The hat is still on his head when Lena finds him. The black WHO DAT shirt, the oatmeal cardigan buttoned one hole off, Keds with the laces dragging, her hair up in a knot she did in the dark. She looks at the hat. Then she looks at him under it. “Goodnight,” she says, “was premature.”

She tucks her hands up into the cardigan sleeves. “Becca Lindell wrote on your wall.” He and Lena have been Facebook friends since the first week of classes, and Becca’s post has been up since Tuesday at 12:41 a.m., two exclamation points and a smiley face, for anybody who cared to look. Somebody cared to look. “It’s a beach cleanup, Jack. It is not a date. Bring gloves.”

journal.title: Fire alarms, 3 a.m.
journal.text: Alarm 1, Monday the 31st, 3:07: everybody on the lawn in what they sleep in; Theo saved the espresso machine; Margot wrote ‘ALARM 1’ like it was a case number. Alarm 2, Friday the 18th, 3:12: eighteen days. Margot says that’s not a schedule, it’s a person. She’s keeping a log.

choices.text: “Gloves are a big step for me.”
response: “Then you’re not ready, Costigan.” She tucks her chin down into the cardigan collar and hums one bar of the Who Dat at the fog.

At 3:36 the strobes quit and the whole building squeaks back across the grass toward the doors. Laney goes in leaning her whole weight on Lena, a parade float being towed home by a much smaller car, and on the way past she lifts her hat off Jack’s head without looking at him and puts it back on her own.
“I’m Newman. I’ll be picking up Las Olas’s sins with tongs.” She considers the fog. “They hand out those grabber sticks. I intend to get one before Joey Abruzzo does, or he’ll grab people.”

At 3:36 the strobes quit and the lawn squeaks back inside. Laney comes out of the fog and drapes herself over Lena from behind, every ounce, and Lena takes it without breaking stride. Going past, Laney lifts the hat off Jack’s head, no look, no thank-you, and puts it back where it belongs.

“I know. I’m the one who said so.” She looks out at the fog. If there’s more coming, the strobes quit at 3:36 before it gets there, and the lawn starts squeaking back across the grass toward the doors.

Laney arrives out of nowhere and hangs her whole weight off Lena’s shoulders, and Lena walks her toward the doors like that, a girl wearing a girl. On the way past, Laney lifts the hat off Jack’s head without a glance and puts it back on her own.

body.title: From: Adrian Hale · To: John Costigan · Thu, Sep 17, 2009, 11:58 PM · Subject: Friday
body.text: Mr. Costigan — Friday, 2:30, my office. Bring the O’Connor in your back pocket; I want to see what a man underlines in it. —A.H.

body: It went to him alone: no cc line, no seminar. For a man who has never once located the BCC field, that’s practically a sealed letter.

Hollis 314 is at the end of the third-floor hall, behind a door with a pebbled-glass pane and HALE in gold leaf that’s been flaking since the second Clinton administration. Inside, the window is the whole Pacific, blue to the top of the glass, the kelp beds dark under the swell. The carpet is a green nobody chose, with a wine stain by the desk in the exact shape of Italy, boot and all. There are shelves, but the books have left them. They stand in stacks on the floor, knee-high, waist-high, with streets between them and one avenue to the desk: a city with no planning board. On the hook behind the door hangs a leash, and there’s no dog.

Hale is in the linen jacket, the wine on the cuff gone the brown of an old map, his reading glasses pushed up into the silver hair. He doesn’t get up. He holds out one hand, palm up, and it takes Jack a second to understand it isn’t for shaking.

He goes through the O’Connor with a licked thumb for every page, as if it were the racing form, and Jack sits across the desk and watches the most famous atheist in California read his margins. Hale reads them out loud. “‘NO.’ ‘Coward.’ ‘Okay, *fine*.’” He looks up over the pages with open delight. “You write in the margins like a man shouting at a referee.” He turns a page. “So did I.”

Then he reaches behind him without looking, into a stack that ought to fall over and doesn’t, and comes out with a paperback: Bernard Williams, *Moral Luck*, Cambridge, 1981, the spine gone soft as an old shirt. He opens it on the desk. Pencil, all down the margins, in a hand thirty years younger than the one across the desk. *No.* Three pages on: *Bernard, really.* “Bring it back,” Hale says, “with your margins in it.”

Jack takes the Benedict holy card out of the O’Connor, where it has been keeping the Misfit’s place since Sunday, and slides it into the Williams. Hale watches the Pope go into Bernard Williams and keeps his face perfectly still. The Williams goes in Jack’s back pocket, where it fits as if it were built for one.

Hale sits back. The chair complains. He folds his hands on his stomach and considers Jack, pleasantly, as if he were a first edition he hadn’t decided to buy. Then, gently, as if asking the time: “You said no. The lucky one doesn’t sleep.” The glasses stay up in his hair. “How would you know, at eighteen?”

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it.

choices.key: You told Hale your brother is in prison.
response: He gives Hale the version he gives anybody who gets one. A fight. A guy got hurt bad. Five years. Danny pleaded.

For once nothing clever is waiting on Hale’s face. What arrives first is plain decency, and it’s a while before anything follows it in. People ask how long. Hale asks, “What do you send him?” “A book a month. Used. They make me erase the margins.”

Hale takes the glasses down out of his hair and holds them by one arm. “Erased,” he says. Then: “That is the most obscene thing I’ve heard this week, and I have read the Baucus draft.” Somewhere under the window a lawnmower starts up and quits. “Thank you for telling me, Mr. Costigan.” He puts the glasses back up on his head, where he’ll lose them by five.

choices.text: “My dad’s been laid off since June. I know what a man looks like who doesn’t sleep.”
response: Hale looks at him across the stacks. “Do you,” he says, and leaves it a statement. He doesn’t push. The pen stays where it’s lying on the blotter. He looks out at the water, and Jack looks at the leash on the hook, and the garage on Glenwood Avenue sits in the room with them, the radio on low, a man in a folding chair at two in the morning.
Then Hale asks what Jack made of Williams’s lorry driver, and they talk about that instead.

“Nobody reads ahead in my class, Mr. Costigan. They read *around*.” He lets Jack have it. He tips back in the complaining chair and enjoys it openly, and the enjoyment is the price: Jack gets out from under the question, and Hale gets to watch him do it.

choices.text: “It’s a seminar, Professor. I argued the side.”
response: “No,” Hale says, “you didn’t.” And then, as if he hadn’t said it, he’s off on Gauguin: Williams’s Gauguin, who leaves a wife and five children for Tahiti, and if the paintings are bad he’s a shit, and if they’re good he’s still a shit but a justified one, and nothing he decided on the dock decides which. “Justified by the weather, Mr. Costigan. Isn’t that monstrous? I’ve loved it for thirty years.”
He talks for a full minute, beautifully, and never once looks at Jack.

body: Theo is cross-legged on his bed in a gray cashmere sweater with the MacBook Pro on his knees, the 5D’s card reader trailing off one side of it and the iPhone tethered to the other, and on the screen is a timeline in Final Cut, stripes of color stacked up like a layer cake. He doesn’t look up. “Sit. Not on the bed. The bed is the edit bay.”

It’s called WEEK ONE, in a title card Theo has spent longer on than any paper: the beach below the bluff that first Friday, firelight, Laney informing the Pacific *who dat*; Sully’s on Sunday, the brass bell, Laney on the table in sequins. The cuts land on the beat. A shot of Kevin catching a falling fry holds exactly as long as it’s funny and not one frame longer. Theo is good at this. Jack can tell how good by how hard he’s working to look bored. “It’s for a class,” Theo says. “What class?” “The class I’m taking in my room.”

Jack takes Theo’s grandfather’s cufflinks out of the top drawer, where they’ve been since Sunday, gold, plain, heavy for their size, and sets them on Theo’s desk. Theo glances over. “Keep them for the Eagles.” “They’re your grandfather’s.” “He’d have liked the Eagles less.” Jack leaves them on the desk anyway, side by side, where Theo can look at them or not.

body: He reads it standing up. Then he turns the RAZR around and holds it out, and Theo takes his hands off the keyboard. “A girl at school said something about Danny,” Jack says. “Gina said his name back.” Theo reads to the end. “Your sister,” he says, “is a killer.” Then the eyebrow. “The nun?” “Nonna’s word. Same girl as the veil girl.”

Theo’s face lights up for about a second: the nun and the veil girl, one girl. Then it goes, and what replaces it is shorter. “Has she met him?” “Thursday. On the bench. She said hi.” Theo nods once. “Good.”

He drags the playhead without asking. “Forty seconds. I was going to wait till it was finished.” He drops it to quarter speed. Sully’s, halftime, from table height: the iPhone propped against the ketchup the whole time, apparently, while Jack thought Theo was just sitting there with his chin on his fist. Lena leaning across the booth with Laney’s gold pencil. Her hand along Jack’s jaw, her thumb at the corner of his mouth. The stroke of gold going on, slow as poured honey at this speed. And Jack, on a laptop screen in Room 412, holding absolutely still, the way you hold still when a bird has landed on you and you’d like it to stay.
Theo freezes it on a frame. “Freeze-frame,” he says. “Very Antoine Doinel. Look at your face, Costigan.” Jack looks. He’d rather not have. Theo keeps his eyes on the screen. “What are you doing?”

choices.key: You told Theo you don’t know what you’re doing.
response: Theo nods slowly. “Okay,” he says. “That’s the right answer. It’s also the worst one.” He saves the cut, Command-S, the little wheel turning, and closes the file.

Then he’s himself again, stretching until his spine cracks. “Sloane Kittredge has invited me to a barn. Tomorrow night, Pi Lam, Laney’s first party as a sister. I’ll be wearing hay.” “I work till one.” “Then come at one. Barns don’t close.”

choices.text: “She’s taken, Theo. I’m not doing anything.”
response: “That’s what I mean,” Theo says, and closes the laptop with one finger. The screen goes, and the room is only the room again, late sun lying across the crucifix over Jack’s bed.

Theo lies back on the edit bay. “Sloane Kittredge has invited me to a barn. Tomorrow night, Pi Lam, Laney’s first party as a sister. I’ll be wearing hay.” “I work till one.” “Then come at one.” He’s already back in the timeline. “Barns don’t close.”

Theo laughs and scrubs back to the top, to the title card, and lets WEEK ONE run again from the beginning, Laney and the Pacific, the bell at Sully’s, every frame of it where he left it. “You’ll need representation,” he says, watching his own cut with frank love.
“Sloane Kittredge has invited me to a barn, by the way. Tomorrow night, Pi Lam, Laney’s first party as a sister. I’ll be wearing hay.” “I work till one.” “Then come at one. Barns don’t close.”

s03b.slug: FRIDAY · 4:20 PM · MISSION STREET, HARBOR SMOKE & CIGAR
body: Harbor Smoke & Cigar has never been within a mile of the harbor. It’s at the near end of Mission Street, where the road comes off Ocean Road past the campus gate, in a stucco strip between a laundromat and a tattoo parlor called Neptune’s. It’s three miles. La Flaca gets him there in twenty minutes, the coaster brake shrieking at every light on Mission.

Inside it’s cedar and cold and dim, the humidors along one wall glowing like aquariums, a bell over the door that goes on faintly ringing after it shuts. Margot is at the counter in black with the peacoat over her arm and a coin purse open on the glass. The clerk, sixties, cardigan, reading glasses on a chain, has been selling her cloves since August, and today he speaks to her softly, as if there’s been a death. “Tuesday,” he says. “The twenty-second. After that it’s menthol or nothing. Congress.” He sets a carton on the glass and rests his palm flat on top of it. “That’s the last Djarum Black between here and San Luis Obispo.”

Margot pays to the cent: bills unfolded from the coin purse one at a time, then quarters, then two dimes, then a nickel she has to dig for. The clerk waits with his hands folded. She takes the carton, turns, and hands it to Jack. “At shoulder height,” she says. “You’re a pallbearer. Conduct yourself.”

Out on the sidewalk she gives him the arrangements. “The wake is Tuesday. The Delgado roof, at sundown. Bring the other Catholic.” She checks the sky. “Rosh Hashanah starts tonight, incidentally. My father observes it as a seminar. There’s a reading list. There’s an apple.” The RAZR has had a text in it since somewhere on Ocean Road. He gets it out.

body: Margot reads it upside down off the RAZR while he’s still reading it right side up, and says nothing about it at all.

She’s going to the chastity talk at Newman tonight. “For the *Tide*,” she says. “There’s no faith page. There will be.” They start for the bus stop at the corner, bearing the carton like a very small casket, at a height she keeps correcting with one finger. Halfway there, without changing her tone in the slightest, she says, “Why wait?” He looks at her. She keeps her eyes on the street. “Actually. Not the pamphlet.”

choices.text: Give her the real case. No pamphlet.
response: So he gives her his own. That the body isn’t a rental. That he isn’t scared of wanting: the wanting is *good*, the wanting is the whole point, it’s about the best thing anybody ever made, and that’s exactly why you don’t hand it out on Mission Street like a flyer for somebody’s band. That he’d like it to mean what it says when he finally says it. He hears himself getting loud on a public sidewalk at four in the afternoon with a carton of clove cigarettes held at shoulder height, and keeps going anyway.

Margot hears him out the whole way to the bus stop. There she takes the carton back. “Lena said the same thing,” she says, “with more Latin.” So they’ve had this one out without him. He finds he’d have paid to watch.

choices.text: “Half the time I don’t know if I can.”
choices.key: You told Margot the truth: half the time you don’t know if you can wait.
response: Margot says nothing. They reach the stop. The bus comes in and kneels at the curb with a long hydraulic sigh, and opens, and waits, and nobody gets on, and the driver gives them a look and closes up and pulls away.

Margot watches it go. “That’s honest,” she says. “From a Catholic. On the subject.” She doesn’t write it down. She takes the carton back out of his hands, carefully, at shoulder height, and holds it against her coat while they wait for the next one.

choices.text: “Cloves are banned in four days. Some of us plan ahead.”
response: Margot nearly laughs. He watches it get as far as the corner of her mouth and get turned back at the border. “Coward,” she says, almost fondly.
At the bus stop she takes the carton back and holds it against her chest, squared and level, like a folded flag.

s04.slug: FRIDAY · 7:30 PM · NEWMAN HOUSE, THE LOUNGE
body: Newman House smells like burnt coffee and powdered sugar. Forty folding chairs face a bedsheet thumbtacked over the shelves of donated books, and a borrowed projector balanced on the ping-pong table — net still dead — throws the title slide up onto it, slightly purple at the edges: LOVE IS PATIENT: OUR CHASTITY STORY, and under that, in a cursive font somebody chose on purpose, *Love is patient and kind. — 1 Cor 13:4.* The 1994 plaid couch has been shoved against the wall to make room. Mrs. Fitch’s lemon bars sit by the door on a paper doily, each one squared off to the next.

Tyler Brandt works the door with a linebacker’s receiving line: a fist bump, a shoulder squeeze, a name. “Brother.” He keeps Jack’s fist a second to make sure it took. “Bridget’s on tech. Sit anywhere. Sit close.” Bridget is a soft-spoken woman in a Franciscan University sweatshirt at the laptop, clicking a test slide forward and back, forward and back, very carefully.

body.text: Margot came in with him. She takes the aisle seat two down from Kevin Tran with her canvas tote on her lap and the carton of Djarum Blacks inside it, her hands folded on top, like the bereaved in the front pew.
body.else: Margot arrives at 7:34, alone, in the black peacoat, with a reporter’s notebook and a pen she clicks once in the doorway — “For the *Tide*” — and takes the aisle seat two down from Kevin Tran as if it had her name on it.

body: Lena is in the back row in the oatmeal cardigan, two lemon bars on a napkin on her knee. She moves her bag off the chair beside her without looking up, and Jack sits in it.

Peter Haddad tells it in his lector voice, in a polo shirt, the clicker in one hand and the other in his pocket, already a congressman. Kenzie Rourke stands beside him, kind and pretty, in a cardigan the projector turns lavender. A Steubenville youth conference, summer 2007: two thousand teenagers and a praise band in a gym in a town Jack has driven through, which is hard to picture anybody falling in love in. Peter saw her across the gym during adoration. “I knew,” he says. “And we chose to wait.” Bridget clicks. Disneyland: the two of them in front of the castle in mouse ears, sunburned and younger, and up through the laptop speakers come Jason Mraz and Colbie Caillat, harmonizing about how lucky they are. Somebody in the third row says *aww* without irony. Kenzie’s cousin’s wedding: Kenzie in sage chiffon, Peter in a rented vest. Peter explains custody of the eyes. He demonstrates it, looking at the floor.

Joey Abruzzo’s hand has been up since the castle. “Is it a sin to think about a girl in a mantilla?” A pause, in which Joey’s face reaches for precision. “*Generally.*” Two rows up a guy in a Cabrillo Hall shirt turns around in his chair to look at Lena. Lena looks back at him until he faces front.

Becca Lindell is front and center with a spiral notebook, a braid down her back as thick as a bell rope. “How do you stay friends with your own body?” she asks. “I grew up around animals. Bodies aren’t the enemy. I don’t want to treat mine like it is.” It is a real question, and Kenzie answers it before Peter can, and well: you feed it and you rest it and you thank it, and you tell it no sometimes, the way you tell anybody you love no. Then Peter lifts the clicker. “And guys —” he aims it at the room — “your future wife is out there *right now*.”
Kevin smiles all the way through that, the whole big smile. Two seats down from him, Margot isn’t looking at the bedsheet. She’s looking at Kevin.

Lena leans an inch toward Jack and says, low, out of the side of her mouth, “It’s true, and they’re selling it like a timeshare.” “Two nights in Orlando,” Jack says, “if you sit through the presentation.”

Q&A. Margot stands. She crosses to the shelf, takes down the lounge’s donated Bible — an Ignatius RSV with a Newman bookplate inside the cover — finds the page without hunting for it, and reads aloud in the voice of a flight attendant doing the exits. “*Wives, be subject to your husbands, as to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church… As the church is subject to Christ, so let wives also be subject in everything to their husbands.*” She keeps a finger in the page. “Kenzie. Do you plan to submit?”

The room makes a sound like a held breath at a free throw. Kenzie crosses the carpet, takes the Bible from Margot — gently, the way you’d take a baby from a stranger — and reads back up the page. “*Be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ.*” Then down it. “*Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.*” She closes it on her own finger. “So yes. I’ll submit to a man exactly as far as he’s already laying his life down for me. And I’ll know how far that is, because he’ll have been doing it every day before anybody asked me.” Margot looks at her. “That’s a better answer than the text deserves,” she says, and sits.
Peter steps in to close it, warm and practical; he has fielded this at three Newman retreats. “Practically? When we can’t agree, I make the call. Prayerfully.”

Kenzie’s smile holds exactly where it is. Her eyes go to the carpet. The silence after that is the long, specific silence of forty Catholics who have all heard the same thing, and it goes on until Kevin Tran is on his feet with Mrs. Fitch’s plate from the door. “Okay! Who’d like to submit to a lemon bar?” The room breaks, grateful, and the plate goes down the row.

Lena turns her head. Jack is already looking at her. The Sunday before either of them left home, August twenty-third, every Catholic church in the country read the same second reading, and it was this one. “Back home,” Jack says, “Father Bruno skipped the homily on it.” “Ours didn’t,” Lena says. They look at each other across an argument with no floor in it. “Not tonight,” she says. “Not tonight,” he says. Up front, Tyler claps once. “Time for one more!”

When Jack faces front again Lena is studying him. Tyler is already thanking everybody for coming.

She makes a small sound through her nose and folds forward over the napkin with her whole body, shoulders going, eyes squeezed shut, while powdered sugar comes down the front of the oatmeal cardigan like a light snow. She gets one hand flat over her mouth and with the other hits Jack in the arm, hard, and keeps her face turned away from him so he can’t see what it’s doing.

She stands a half step behind Peter with the Bible still closed on her finger, smiling when the room laughs, and between laughs her face empties out the way a face does at the end of a double shift. She keeps the smile ready for the next laugh, and it comes, and she puts the smile on for it, and she is so tired that for a second Jack has to look at the bedsheet instead.

s04b.slug: FRIDAY · 9:04 PM · NEWMAN HOUSE, THE FRONT STEPS
body: Becca catches him in the doorway with the spiral notebook against her chest and a pen behind her ear. “Nine a.m. Campus Point. You’re on my team.” She taps the notebook where his name presumably is. “I put you down.” And she’s gone back inside to help Bridget wind up the extension cord before he can tell her he owns no gloves.

Out on the steps the Grove is all creak and menthol in the dark. Margot lights a clove — four days left of legal — and points it at Lena. “My problem isn’t the theology. The theology I can at least footnote. My problem is that every slide was about a girl as a present. Wrapped. Kept nice. Commodified — yes, I said commodified, I’m in college. Handed to the right man on the right day so he can open her. Which means the girls who don’t make it to the day are damaged goods, and you know who pays for that? Not Peter. Peter gets forgiven by the third slide. And the one sentence they aimed at the boys was about a girl. *Your future wife is out there.* Not one slide about what the boys do.”

“You’re right about the boys,” Lena says at once. “And you’re right about who pays. I went to an all-girls school, Margot, I watched who paid.” She comes down a step to be level with her. “You’re wrong about the present. Nobody *unwraps* you. *Gaudium et spes*, twenty-four: man cannot fully find himself except through a sincere gift of himself. *Of* himself, Margot. The self does the giving, when she decides to, because it’s hers — that’s the whole point of calling it a gift. The slideshow got that wrong, and you took the slideshow’s word for it.” Margot exhales clove at the eucalyptus. “I’m quoting you.” “Spell Broussard right.”

body.text: Margot reaches into the tote and lays the carton across Jack’s forearms. “Pallbearer duties resume Tuesday.” Then she and Lena go down the steps together toward Ocean Road, still at it, the clove smoke going on ahead of them, and Jack stands under the porch light holding twenty packs of contraband at shoulder height, as instructed.

s05.slug: SATURDAY · 8:52 AM · CAMPUS POINT, THE BEACH
body: The marine layer sits on Campus Point like a lid. Low tide has pulled the water back a long way and left a wrack line the length of the beach: kelp in brown ropes, sand fleas going up off it in little bursts, bottle caps, a pink flip-flop, a snarl of fishing line with the hook still in it, and cigarette butts by the hundred, ground into the sand like seeds. Some of them are Reds. Jack picks those up first.

Forty volunteers in matching gray shirts — ST. BRENDAN’S · CARE FOR CREATION — stand around five-gallon buckets with trash grabbers, and somewhere in one of the buckets Joey Abruzzo’s iPod speaker is playing Kings of Leon, the bucket making it sound like a stadium in a cave. It’s the state’s Coastal Cleanup Day too; Becca registered the site, and the tally card is clipped to her clipboard under the sign-in sheet.

Becca has the clipboard and a whistle she does with her teeth and her tongue, no hands, that could move a herd off a county road. Before she can get to Jack with the spare gloves, Kevin Tran is in front of him holding out a pair of gray canvas work gloves, new, the price sticker still on the cuff. “I brought six,” Kevin says. “I’m a planner.” Becca arrives a step behind with a pink pair held out. “Next time,” she says, and makes a note.

She does the pairings off the clipboard. Kevin with Bridget, who has her sleeves rolled and a bucket on each arm. Lena with Joey, thirty yards down the sand. Becca with Jack. “Seating chart,” she says, without a blush.

So he works beside Becca Lindell for two hours, and it is not a date, and she treats it like one with total, cheerful frankness. She asks how many kids he wants, and when he says he’s never thought about a number she tells him hers. “Seven. Or nine.” She bags a Styrofoam cup. “Odd numbers, so there’s a tiebreaker.” “What are they voting on?” “Everything. Dinner. Names. Whether Dad gets to sell the truck.” Five brothers and two sisters, and the oldest sister’s the one you’d be scared of. A ranch on the Rathdrum road. A calf she pulled at twelve, in February, in the dark, by flashlight, her arm in to the shoulder and her father holding the light and saying *pull* and *wait* and *pull*. She tells it the way other girls tell the plot of a movie. Then she asks him about his prayer life, and she asks it like a person, not like Tyler. “What do you pray when you can’t think?” “Hail Mary,” Jack says. “It runs on its own.” Becca nods. “Glory Be, for me. It’s short. You can get through it while a cow’s kicking you.”

Thirty yards down, Joey’s voice carries without trying: Dunwoodie, a girl from Cabrillo with a nose ring, Dunwoodie again. Lena is in sight the whole time, a fixed point in the long gray morning, bending, straightening, her hair tied up in a cotton scarf against the damp.

Near the bluff, in the kelp, something small and clear catches the light — collapsed, glistening, the size of a fist. Jack has been reading about the moon jellies that wash up after a spring tide. He gets it with the grabber, carefully, so as not to tear it, and lifts it up to show her.
It is not a jellyfish. It is, unmistakably, Friday night on Las Olas.

Becca looks at it on the end of his grabber. Then she reaches over, takes it off the jaws with her gloved hand, and drops it in her bag. “I’ve pulled a calf,” she says. “Give it here.” Thirty yards down the beach, Lena, who saw the whole thing, sits straight down in the wet sand, laughing, while Joey asks what’s funny.

Later she comes up the beach toward the buckets with a full bag over her shoulder and sand on the seat of her jeans, and doesn’t slow down. “*Caritas in Veritate,* forty-eight,” she says, passing. “The Pope says the beach is a gift.” “Forty-eight through fifty-one,” says Jack, who has the encyclical in a milk crate under his bed. Lena considers the grabber in his hand, and what it was holding an hour ago. “He’s right about the beach,” she says. “I’ll give him the beach.” She keeps going.

At noon the fog starts to lift and Becca blows the whistle. They rinse the grabbers at the waterline, shin-deep, the Pacific so cold it aches in the ankle bones, sand going out from under their heels with every wave. Becca wrings out the hem of her shirt and looks at him sideways with the water around them. “How’d you get the scar?”

choices.key: You told Becca the scar came from walking into the Pacific.
response: Becca looks down at the Pacific Ocean, which is currently around both their shins. She looks at his eyebrow. She looks at the Pacific again.
“That’s a lie,” she says. “Is it a nice lie?” She lets a wave go past. “Because I don’t mind a nice one, as long as I get the real one later.”

choices.key: You told Becca a Franciscan gave you the scar in a pickup game.
response: He gives her the friar: a brown habit hiked up into a rope belt, sandals on blacktop, an elbow he never saw coming. Becca’s whole face opens.

“My brother Eli lost a front tooth to a Benedictine,” she says. “Church picnic. Volleyball. Father Anselm. He still says he was going for the ball.” She shakes water off the grabber. “It’s always the monks. Nobody warns you about the monks.”

choices.key: You told Becca part of the truth: a fight, a long time ago.
response: She takes it straight, like everything else this morning. She nods once, a short ranch nod, and rinses the grabber jaws in the next wave.
“Okay,” Becca says. They walk up out of the water with their jeans dark to the knee, and she bumps his shoulder with hers, once, going up the sand.
Becca isn’t put off in the slightest. She tucks the clipboard under her arm, out of the spray.
“I like long stories,” she says. “I grew up with no TV and ten people at dinner. Later.” And she writes something on the back of the tally card that he can’t read from where he’s standing.

body: The Welcome BBQ is a rented propane grill, a folding table of hot dogs and burgers and veggie patties sweating in their plastic, two watermelons, a Costco sheet cake that says WELCOME HOME in blue gel, lemonade in orange coolers, and name tags on masking tape. In the shade of the olive tree a sophomore with a guitar is working through “All Are Welcome” for the third time, with feeling.

Fr. Osei has the grill, clerical shirt, sleeves rolled, the rubber boots on. He raises the tongs for silence and begins the grace, and halfway through it the 1962 sprinkler under the olive tree coughs twice and comes on full, and soaks the potato salad, the guitarist and the front of the line. Osei finishes the grace without hurrying. Then he looks at the sprinkler with great affection. “Even the sprinkler is Catholic,” he says. “It could not wait for the Amen.”
Tyler finds Jack in the line, wet to the elbow. “Coffee. This week. Your prayer life.” “Wednesday,” Jack says, and Tyler fist-bumps him like Jack has signed with his team.

Mrs. Fitch has a table of her own by the rectory steps, the lemon bars in rows, and when Jack comes around the end of the line with two hot dogs she has company: Lena with a paper plate, Bridget, a pair of nursing girls, and Becca, sunburned along the part of her hair, with her back to him. “I told my mother this was a date,” Becca is telling the table, cheerfully, cutting a lemon bar in half with a plastic knife. “She’s very happy. She’s lighting a candle in Coeur d’Alene.” Mrs. Fitch says *how lovely*. Across the table Lena looks down at her lemon bar and cuts it into very small pieces. Becca, her back to Jack the whole time, is already asking who wants the corner piece.

A minute later Kenzie Rourke sits down at the other end of it and sets a second plate beside him — a burger, potato salad from the dry side. She looks at the courtyard, not at him. “Good question,” she says quietly. “Nobody asks that one.” Then she gets up and goes back to the cake table. Across the courtyard Peter is in a circle of juniors, laughing a little longer than the joke.

body: When the line thins, Osei waves him over to the grill. He turns burgers without saying anything, the fat spitting, the reading glasses down on their cord. “Your grandmother’s Mass is Tuesday at twelve-ten,” he says. “I will say it myself.” He flips one. Then he puts the glasses on and looks at Jack over them, a doctor’s look, unhurried, the look that goes straight past the patient’s account of himself to the chart. “You are carrying something heavier than a trash bag this week.”

response: Osei sets the spatula down. “How?”

So Jack tells him, with the grill hissing: a girl at Gina’s school who said something about his brother, in front of the class; and Gina, fifteen, saying his name back to her; and the other girl looking away first. Osei listens as if there were nothing else on the grill.
“Ɛyɛ,” he says at last. “It is well.” He picks up the spatula. “Then we will pray for the other girl too. She will need it more.”
Osei laughs, the tongs held up out of the way. Two of the nursing girls look over from Mrs. Fitch’s table to see what’s funny.

“Ah,” he says, wiping his eye with his wrist. “That too.” And he goes back to the burgers, still smiling at them, and asks Jack whether Ohio people put ketchup on a hot dog, because he has heard terrible things.
“Good,” Osei says. He flips a burger. It lands right where it was. “Tuesday, twelve-ten.”
He slides a cheeseburger onto Jack’s empty plate without asking whether he wants one, and turns to the next person in line.

s06b.slug: SATURDAY · 3:50 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S COURTYARD, THE OLIVE TREE
body: The cleanup of the cleanup. The courtyard is down to paper plates in the hedges and a Costco cake with one corner left. The coat-closet door in the church has been shut since three-thirty, a line of four on the bench outside it. Jack and Becca fold the last tables in the shade of the olive tree, his end and her end, the legs snapping in with a sound like a staple gun.
She leans the table against the trunk. Then she says it, with no lead-in, to his face. “I told my mother this was a date. She’s very happy.” She wipes her hands on her jeans. “Was it?”

journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer; has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wants a second. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard.

He tells her he can’t do Saturday nights; he washes dishes at the Anchor, seven to one. She didn’t know. s07.slug: SATURDAY · 5:10 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE MAILBOXES
body: The lobby at ten past five smells like the basement laundry has been coming up the elevator shaft all afternoon, sweet and chemical. Marcus is at the front desk behind a yellow highlighter and the organic chemistry book, and he has highlighted so much of the open page that it has gone back to meaning nothing. Jack’s hair is still wet from the fourth-floor shower, and there’s sand in the cuffs of his jeans he’ll be finding till Tuesday. Box 412: a Sigma Rho car-wash flyer, a credit-card offer that calls Theodore A. Vance a valued customer, and an envelope addressed in pencil, block capitals, pressed so hard the letters stand up on the back. In the corner, smaller, the same hand:

body.title: Envelope, top left corner
body.text:

A555218
TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION
LEAVITTSBURG, OHIO 44430

body: He doesn’t open it in the lobby. He takes the east stairs instead of the elevator, two at a time to four, where the concrete repeats every footstep half a second late, and sits on the top step of the landing under the window that opens six inches. The Lagoon in the slot. One bar on the RAZR. Nobody. He opens the envelope with his thumb.

body.title: Lined paper, pencil, both sides
body.text:
Professor —
Your ocean letter got here Tuesday. Sixty-six degrees, green on top and gray underneath. I read it to Reggie twice. Reggie’s from Portsmouth, he’s seen the Ohio River, he says same thing. Reggie wants to know does the Pacific smell. Find out and report back, that’s an order.
Brideshead is still in the mailroom. I think a C.O. is reading it. Good for him honestly.
I called the house tonight and Gina picked up and said everything’s fine. Everything’s fine, Danny. She’s been saying fine since she was four years old, that’s how I know it ain’t. You know what it is. Don’t tell me. Tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. I got it.
Tell the veil girl thanks for asking my name. Nobody out there asks it anymore. They ask Ma how I’m doing like I’m the weather.
Send the Hopkins. Ma says it’s poems. Send it anyway.
Ma says you sound skinny on the phone. Eat something.
—D.

body: Maybe that’s what it was. Thursday on the bluff bench the recorded woman came in over his brother at *tell Gina —* and took the rest of the sentence back to Leavittsburg with her. Danny called the house Wednesday night. This was already in the mail.

Out through the six inches of open window the Lagoon is going pewter. Something small and dark — a coot, a grebe; he’s from Youngstown, it’s a duck — draws a line across the water that closes up behind it. Jack keeps his thumb on the fold until the line is gone. Then he folds the letter along Danny’s creases and puts it in his back pocket, flat against Hale’s Williams.

At twenty to six he wedges the RAZR into the top corner of the window frame, where the bar lives, and calls home. Twenty to nine on Glenwood Avenue. His mother picks up on the second ring, the dishwasher going behind her. “Did you eat? Don’t lie, I can hear it.” “Two hot dogs. A priest grilled them.” “A priest,” she repeats, impressed and suspicious at once. Nonna told Father Bruno about the rectory Mass, she reports, in the vestibule after the eight o’clock, where the Iannuccis could hear; Father Bruno says tell him good. Ohio State won. “Your father yelled at the TV, Jackie. In a good way.” Then, in a different voice: “It’s the nineteenth. She lit the candle for Nonno this morning.”
Jack knows what the nineteenth is. Nineteen seventy-seven, a Monday: Sheet & Tube shut the Campbell Works, and Nonno came home before ten with his lunch still in the pail.

A click, the extension in the front room, and the post-game show comes in behind it, two men in sport coats laughing. “Thirty-eight nothing,” his father says. “In Cleveland. You see that?” “I saw it.” He didn’t; he was at a church barbecue with a sprinkler. His father breathes into the phone. “Good. Don’t waste it.” Click.
Then a scuffle at the kitchen end, a chair leg, his mother saying *Regina*, and Gina has the phone. “is the nun’s name a secret —” And his mother has it back. “Nonna wants you.”
The extension in Nonna’s room, three tries, EWTN behind her and a rosary in progress. “Giacomino.” Thin and fierce as a wire. “E la ragazza? The nun?”

So he tells her. The nun painted a fleur-de-lis on his face for the football, and he wore it to Communion by accident. The nun’s team hasn’t lost. The nun said hi to Danny on the telephone, and Danny laughed. Nonna laughs at all of it, the old laugh with the cough on the end, and at the last one she stops and says, “She talk to Danny,” not asking. Then: “Brava. Brava la monaca.”

Then Rosie, thirty seconds, breathless, about the drawing she mailed Tuesday: it’s him at the beach, the orange part is the sun and the other orange part is a crab, and he has to put it on his wall *today*. He promises. Then his mother again — the Iannuccis’ new dog, which is the size of a loaf of bread and hates Frank — and a rustle on the line, and the extension lifting in Nonna’s room. Three tries. The rosary going behind her.
“Giacomino.” The same voice. The same words. “E la ragazza? The nun?”
She’s asking it new. On the kitchen end, his mother has gone quiet.

journal.title: Danny
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; a C.O. is reading it first. The ocean letter got there; he read it to Reggie, from Portsmouth, who wants to know if the Pacific smells. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down Wednesday night: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. Thanked the veil girl for asking his name.

choices.text: Answer her again. The same, like it’s the first time.

response: So he tells it again. The fleur-de-lis, the Communion line, the team that hasn’t lost, Danny laughing — the same jokes in the same order, with the same pauses where she laughed the first time. She laughs in the same places. At the end she says, “Brava. Brava la monaca,” exactly as before, and he says, “I’ll tell her, Nonna,” as if he hadn’t said it five minutes ago.
Then the rustle, and his mother’s voice, close: “She’s tired, honey.”

A pause with EWTN in it. “So I ask again,” Nonna says. “I’m old, I’m allowed.” She says it fondly, the way she says everything to him, and he can hear in it that she has no idea why he said what he said. Then she wants to know about the girl.
Then the rustle, and his mother’s voice, close: “She’s tired, honey.”
He says it gently. It doesn’t take any doing; his mother is already reaching for the phone, he can hear her crossing the kitchen. “She’s tired, honey.”

body: Saturday at the Anchor runs on a different engine from Tuesday. By midnight every booth is Las Olas kids sobering up on hash browns, the Hobart slams its hood every ninety seconds, and the steam has made a weather system of the dish pit that Jack lives inside with his sleeves shoved past the elbow. Somebody in booth six has found the jukebox’s one Mariah Carey and paid to hear it three times.

PIE OF THE DAY, says the chalkboard: KEY LIME. Gloria stops at the pass with the coffee pot and looks back out at booth four, where a boy and a girl in matching Sigma Rho sweatshirts are sharing one slice with two forks and not looking at each other. “Key lime,” she tells Jack, about them. “Looks like a good time, and it’ll make your face do that.” She does the face. It is exactly the face. Then she’s through the door again with the pot.

Rudy has the transistor off tonight — Saturday is too loud for Vin Scully — and a Louis L’Amour in his apron with the spine taped. At ten to twelve, flipping eggs for a table of surfers, he says without turning around, “You wrote him?” “He wrote back.” Rudy nods at the flattop as though the eggs had told him something good. He slides two of them, over easy, onto a plate with rye toast, cut on the diagonal, and sets it on the steel by the Hobart. “Dish man eats.”

At 12:40 the bell over the door, and Rafi Ochoa, skateboard under one arm and a backpack on both shoulders, his hair stiff with salt. He takes a stool at the counter, orders the key lime, and counts exact change onto the Formica. When Jack comes out with a rack of clean mugs, Rafi lifts his fork. “Boss.” His family’s place is two blocks up the hill from the wharf; his abuela’s asleep, and what she doesn’t know about pie can’t hurt her. He looks at the clock over the register. “You off at one? I’ll skate you out as far as Las Olas. I got deliveries on Seacliff.”
At 1:12, mopping under the Hobart, Jack feels the RAZR go off in his apron pocket.

He folds the phone and hangs up the apron and has La Flaca off the wharf rail before Gloria can rate his exit. Rafi drops the board, catches the wire basket with one hand going by, and they’re moving.

body: La Flaca has no light. She came to him the first week of September with a basket and a chain and a seat that tilts and no light, and for two and a half weeks Jack has ridden Ocean Road home at one in the morning by the white line and memory. Tonight Rafi is behind him on the skateboard with one hand on the wire basket, getting towed, his wheels ticking over every seam in the asphalt. The fog is down to the road. Past the turnoff for St. Brendan’s the Grove starts on the right, the eucalyptus creaking in it and letting go of long strips of bark onto the shoulder.

Headlights come up behind them, slow, and stay slow. Then a light starts turning on the inside of a windshield, red and blue in the fog, and a gray Crown Victoria with no markings and a long antenna eases up level with La Flaca’s back wheel and keeps pace.

The driver’s window comes down. A man in a navy windbreaker leans an elbow out — fifties, by the face; gray in the mustache; a gold badge clipped to his belt that the dome light finds. He holds a badge wallet out the window, open, at reading distance: the shield, and under a photo with more hair, DETECTIVE SERGEANT. “Ray Ochoa. Marisol Police.” He gives Jack time to read it. “License and registration.”
To a bicycle.

Jack stops La Flaca on the coaster brake and puts a foot down. Then, because something has to be done and nothing else occurs to him, he works his wallet out of his back pocket from behind the Williams and Danny’s letter and hands over his Ohio driver’s license. The man takes it. He holds it up into the dome light and reads it like the Gospel. “John Anthony Costigan,” he says. “Youngstown.”
“Pop,” says Rafi, coasting up into the light on the board.

The man doesn’t look at his son. He’s still looking at the license. “I know that board from a quarter mile back, Rafael. I paid for that board.” He’s on call, it turns out, westbound, a car break-in on Del Playa. “It’ll keep. That car’s been getting broken into since 1987.” Then something to Rafi in Spanish, fast and low, of which Jack catches *la luz* and *tu abuela* and nothing else, and Rafi answers in Spanish with both palms up.

Ray turns back. “California Vehicle Code, twenty-one two-oh-one, subsection d. A bicycle operated during darkness shall be equipped with a lamp emitting a white light visible from a distance of three hundred feet in front.” More or less; he recites it flat, in one breath. He looks at La Flaca, at the rust and the basket and the tilted seat. “This bicycle was reported abandoned at the harbor in 2007.”
“Not stolen,” Rafi says. “Abandoned. Abuela says there’s a week’s difference.”
“Your abuela is not a court.” Ray hands the license back through the window, and on the way he takes a better look at Jack’s face. “You’re Gloria’s dish man. Rudy’s kitchen.”
And Jack has him, then: Tuesdays, the far end of the counter, meatloaf and black coffee, a man who nods to Rudy through the pass and never says a word to him.

response: “Detective,” Ray says, correcting him, warm, almost pleased, and for the first time something in the tired face moves — the mustache, mostly. Rafi, behind Jack, makes a small noise of professional admiration.

choices.text: “It’s his bike. I don’t have a light. That’s on me.”
choices.key: Stopped by Rafi’s father on Ocean Road, you owned the missing light.
response: Ray looks at him through the window with the dome light on both of them, and keeps looking, until Jack starts to wonder if there’s a form. “Huh,” Ray says finally. Rafi looks at Jack as if he’s done something illegal and beautiful.

choices.text: “Is this about the light or the bike?”
response: “It’s about your mouth, Mr. Costigan,” Ray says, without heat, as though it were subsection e. Behind Jack, Rafi is delighted and says absolutely nothing, which is its own kind of noise.

choices.text: Hands on the bars. Say nothing.
response: Jack keeps his hands on the bars where they can be seen and his mouth shut. Ray considers this. Then, to Rafi, in English: “See that? He knows how to get pulled over. You could learn.”

body: Ray looks past him, at Rafi, at the backpack on Rafi’s shoulders. “What’s in the bag, Rafael?”
“Vitamins, Pop.”
Ray looks at his son. It goes on long enough for the dash light to come around four or five times on the side of Rafi’s face, red, blue, red. Then he looks away from the bag.

He puts the car in park and gets out, a hand on the door frame for his knees, and walks back to the trunk, and comes back with a clip-on bike light still on its cardboard. “Found property,” he says. “It’s been found.” He bends over La Flaca’s handlebar and clips it on himself, tests the clamp, and clicks it on, and a cone of white light goes out ahead of them into the fog and gives them twenty feet of Ocean Road they didn’t have before.

Back at the car he leans on the roof and looks at Jack. “He selling you anything?” “No, sir.” It’s the truth. Ray nods. Then he looks off down Ocean Road toward the Grove, toward the dark where the road bends. “I’ve picked enough kids up off this road.”

He gets in. The dash light goes off. The Crown Vic pulls ahead, unhurried, toward Del Playa and the car that’s been getting broken into since 1987, and its taillights go small and red in the fog, and then there’s only the fog.

They roll again. Rafi on the board with one hand on the basket, the new light swinging a little on the bars and laying a white path down for them to ride on. After a hundred yards: “Thanks, boss.” And then, though Jack hasn’t asked and wasn’t going to — Rafi is straight about anything that costs money, whatever it is — “Weed. Adderall around midterms. Not bars, though. I don’t do bars anymore.”

journal.title: Rafi Ochoa (204)
journal.text: Rafi Ochoa. Second floor. Carried my fridge up four flights and was gone before Dad could tip him. Calls everybody boss. Lent me his bike on the wharf at one in the morning like it was nothing, till Christmas. His father’s a detective. He sells weed, and Adderall around midterms. Not bars, he says.

journal.title: Ray Ochoa (Marisol PD)
journal.text: Detective Sergeant, per the badge wallet. Rafi’s father. Gray Crown Vic, a windbreaker, the Vehicle Code by heart. Knows my face from the Anchor counter: Tuesdays, meatloaf, a nod to Rudy. Did the bit: ‘License and registration.’ Asked what was in the bag and took ‘vitamins’ for an answer. Gave me a light out of his trunk. Found property.

response: “Yeah,” Rafi says. He rides on that, the board humming. “He’s a good one. That’s the problem.”
At the top of Seacliff he lets go of the basket with a little push and peels off west toward the surf rentals and his deliveries. The new light carries Jack the last two blocks to Pi Lam alone.
Rafi grins at the fog. “My abuela says the devil’s patient, so be faster.”

Jack rides. A block goes by under the light, then most of another. “Appreciate you, boss,” Rafi says.

s09.slug: SUNDAY · 1:52 AM · SEACLIFF ROAD, PI LAMBDA CHI, THE PORCH STEPS
body: Pi Lambda Chi at ten to two in the morning: the white colonial with the black shutters and the best porch on Seacliff Road, the porch strung with Christmas lights and stacked with hay bales, a bedsheet banner — PI LAM RODEO — sagging off the second-floor rail. Kid Cudi is coming out the open front door, and the bass comes with him, down through the porch boards and the steps and up through the soles of Jack’s shoes. Two Sigma Rho boys in borrowed straw hats are trying to rope a plastic lawn flamingo with a phone charger. The whole house smells of hay, Natty Light and the jasmine on the neighbor’s fence. Jack locks La Flaca to the porch rail and clicks Ray’s light off to save the battery.

Lena is on the bottom step in a blue cotton dress and the oatmeal cardigan, barefoot, the brown Justins standing side by side on the step beside her like two people waiting for a ride. She has a red Solo cup, and when she sees him she lifts it an inch. Water. Proof, or a toast.

Through the doorway he can see the stairs. Laney is going up them, more or less, steered at each elbow by a sister in a bandana, with Sloane Kittredge one step behind and a hand flat between her shoulder blades: clipboard energy at two in the morning, no clipboard required. The pink hat is gone. There’s hay in Laney’s hair and her mascara has started south and she has never looked more like herself. She finds Jack over the banister. “*FIREMAN.*” The sisters keep steering. “I’m not a mess, sugar,” she calls down. “I’m a *destination*.” Then her arm comes over the banister, and one finger, aimed at the bottom step. “Take her home, fireman. She’s being a *mother*.” She says it laughing. It comes down the stairs anyway and lands on the step, and Lena looks at the water in her cup. Sloane leans over the rail, kind and entirely final. “We’ve got her,” she tells Lena. “She’s ours now.” Then the landing takes the three of them, and a door upstairs shuts on the music.

Theo is leaning in the doorway in black cashmere with hay all over it. Sloane’s hand was on his arm until she went up the stairs, and then it wasn’t. He looks up the stairwell after them. “I’ll stay,” he says. Then, to Lena, easily, as if it were nothing: “I’m up anyway.”

Lena is on her feet. She gives it to him fast and exact, one item at a time, the way she reads out a citation. “On her side. Not her back — her *side*. Water by the bed, and make her drink half of it before she sleeps. She had one of her pills at eleven — *one*, she says — and vodka after. If her breathing — ”
“I know what to look for,” Theo says. He goes in and takes the stairs two at a time.
Then it’s just the porch light and the hay and the bass in the boards. Lena stands on the step and looks at the empty doorway until the song changes.

body.text: Then she turns around and looks at him. “I said *request*.”

body: She bends and picks the boots up by their pull-straps and doesn’t put them on. “Walk me home, Costigan,” she says. “The long way.” And she turns east.

response: He holds out his hand. She looks at it, and at him, and gives them over: two old brown Justins, resoled twice, warm from the step and heavier than they look. He hooks both pull-straps over his fingers, and that’s how he carries them, from here on, all the way.
“Not tonight it isn’t,” Lena says. She is already walking east, the boots swinging from one hand, and he goes after her.

He falls in beside her. She swings the boots by their straps as she walks, in time with the bass until the bass is a block behind them, and then in time with the surf coming up at the end of the street.

s09b.slug: SUNDAY · 2:06 AM · THE BEACH BELOW LAS OLAS
body: The bluff stairs go down from Seacliff below the bench where she said hi to his brother on Thursday: wooden treads with sand on every one, a handrail furred with salt, a hundred-odd steps into the dark. Then the beach. It’s two nights past the new moon and there is no moon at all. The stars go clear down to the water, more of them than Youngstown has ever been allowed, and offshore the whole glow of the town lies smeared orange across a fog bank that hasn’t made up its mind to come in. The sand at the wash line is packed hard and cold enough to ache. Lena walks down in the wash, where it’s wettest, and lets the Pacific come up as far as it likes.

At 2:10 the horn comes off the bluff right over their heads. Two long, one short, one long. Then the freight itself, so close above them in the dark that the sand under Jack’s shoes takes a share of the weight: car after car after car, steel on steel up there past the lip of the bluff. He knows how this goes. The number starts on its own, one car into the next, the way it has since he was six. He doesn’t let it. Beside him in the wash Lena’s mouth is still. Neither of them counts. It is the longest train he has ever heard, and it goes over them uncounted, every car of it, and thins away north up the coast, and the surf comes back up the beach to fill the place where it was.
“She has sisters now,” Lena says.

She walks a few more yards. “Thursday she ran across Seacliff to me first. Across the whole street, in a hat, through sixty girls screaming. I watched her pick me out.” The wash runs up white and slides back. “Tonight she didn’t need anybody to run to. Which is good. Which is what she wanted, and it’s good.” She kicks at the foam. “I’m not her mother.”

choices.text: “She ran to you first. That’s not a Thursday thing.”
response: Lena walks on that for the length of three waves, and when she does say something, it’s about the water. “It’s colder than the Gulf,” she says. “The Gulf in September is a bathtub somebody forgot to drain.” But she’s walking a foot nearer to him than she was.

choices.text: “She called you a mother because hers is the one she’s scared of.”
response: Lena stops in the wash. The water goes out around her and pulls the sand from under her, and she lets it. She heard the voicemail too, on Wednesday, on the floor of 217: *Delaney Rose. Posture, sweetheart.* “I know,” she says. “That’s why it worked.”

He does Laney: the Dallas vowels, the hip, one hand on top of a hat that isn’t there. Lena laughs out loud, a bark that goes off down the empty beach and startles something in the kelp, and she points at him. “*Don’t* do her,” she says. “You do her better than I do.”

s09c.slug: SUNDAY · 2:18 AM · THE CREEK MOUTH, BELOW THE GROVE
body: They hear it before they see it: a low, steady tearing in the dark ahead, louder than the surf and nothing like it. Then it’s at their feet — the Lagoon’s outlet coming out from under the Grove, black and moving and full of broken starlight, spread across the beach in a sheet that braids and unbraids on its way to the sea. The air off it is ten degrees colder and smells of eucalyptus and mud. The noise of it fills up the place where talking was.

body.text: Her boots hang from his left hand by their straps.
body.else: She has the boots in her left hand by their straps.

body: He doesn’t bother with his shoes. They’re Anchor shoes; they’ve been wetter. He rolls his jeans to the shin, and she gathers the blue dress up at the knee in her free hand, and the two of them stand on the edge and look at the water, and the water goes on not caring.

choices.key: At the creek mouth you offered Lena your arm, and she took it.
response: He crooks his right arm and holds it out, an usher at a wedding. She looks at it. Then she puts her hand on his forearm, and they go in.

The cold takes him at the shins like a dropped wrench. Her fingers close through the flannel on the first step and don’t let go, and she tests every stone before she trusts it, and halfway over one rolls under her and her grip goes hard, and for two steps all her weight is on his arm and the whole warm side of her is against him — hay, salt, her hair at his jaw — and keeping his arm an arm, and not letting it become a hand at her waist, costs him exactly everything he carried into the water. Then the far bank. She lets go. She shakes the creek off one leg like a cat and walks on up the sand.

choices.key: At the creek mouth you went first and didn’t look back. She took your sleeve anyway.
response: He goes in first. The cold takes him at the shins and climbs. He doesn’t look back; he listens to her come in behind him — the splash, the hiss through her teeth, a word in French that no nun ever taught anybody — and keeps his eyes on the far bank.

Halfway, her fingers close on his sleeve from behind, a fistful of flannel at the elbow, and hold on. Not turning around costs him more than he would have believed eleven inches of water could charge: to keep facing the dark bank with her hand knotted in his sleeve and her breath at his shoulder blade, and walk, and keep walking. On the far bank she lets go of the sleeve as though she never had it.

choices.key: You offered to carry Lena across the creek. She declined, with threats.
response: “Costigan,” she says, “I *will* drown you in eleven inches of water.”

She wades. He goes in a yard downstream of her to make a point, and the channel shelves off under him and takes him to the knee, and the cold goes up the denim like bad news. On the far bank she reaches out and steadies herself on his shoulder for the one step up out of the soft sand, her whole palm flat on him through the flannel, and he stands as still as a fence post and lets himself be a fence post, and it costs him more than the water did. Then she gets a look at his jeans, black to the knee and streaming, and laughs at them all the way up the beach.

s10.slug: SUNDAY · 2:31 AM · CAMPUS POINT, THE LIFEGUARD TOWER
body: The lifeguard tower at Campus Point has been closed since Labor Day. It stands up on the sand on its pilings like a shed somebody forgot to take home: a plywood shutter chained across the window, a sun-bleached sign — NO LIFEGUARD ON DUTY — and a wooden ramp down to the beach, where they sit, a foot of splintered gray boards between them. The wind off the water works at the shutter, and the chain lets it go an inch and catches it, over and over, a small dry knock behind their heads. Out past the sand the beginner break folds over in the dark, pale where it breaks, and then not.

body.text: His jeans squeak when he sits. Lena listens to them with enormous interest. “You *squeak*, Costigan.” She is nowhere near done enjoying it.

body: She pulls the cardigan down over her knees. Then, conversationally, like the weather: “Becca Lindell told my lemon bar she told her mother.” He waits. “She’s lighting a candle in Coeur d’Alene, Costigan. There is a woman in Idaho on her knees about you.”

body.text: “I told you at three in the morning it wasn’t a date,” she says, “and you agreed with me. I’d like to know which of us was wrong.”

body: She turns her head on her knees and looks at him. “Was it?”

choices.text: “It seemed like the right thing to want.”
response: “That’s the worst reason I’ve ever heard, Costigan,” Lena says, “and I’ve heard you defend the Browns.” The shutter knocks twice. Then, lower, and not for her own sake — he can hear whose sake it’s for: “She told a whole table the truth on the first date. In front of Mrs. Fitch. Do you know how rare that is? That’s okra in California.” She looks at him straight. “Don’t be careless with her.”

choices.text: “She’s lovely. I don’t know what I’m doing.”
response: “She *is* lovely,” Lena says, and means every word. “She pulled a calf at twelve and told me about it like it was a recipe.” She works a splinter loose from the ramp and flicks it into the dark. “Then find out what you’re doing. Before she does.” And, plainer: “Don’t be careless with her.”

choices.text: “It was a beach cleanup. I have it in writing. From you.”
response: “I said it wasn’t a date,” Lena says. “I didn’t say I was right.” She tips her head at him on her knees, pleased with herself, and he has nothing, and the shutter knocks, and she waits, very politely, while he looks for something, and the shutter knocks again, and the round is hers.

s10b.slug: SUNDAY · 3:08 AM · THE MARINE LAB STAIRS
body: The Marine Lab sits dark at the foot of the bluff with its back to the sea, and the stairs go up beside it: concrete, a pipe rail beaded wet, a caged bulb on every landing. Behind a steel door on the first landing something electric hums, low and steady — the touch-tank pump, moving the ocean around in the dark for the anemones all night, whether anybody comes to look or not.

body.text: For the first flight she is formal. “Mind the step, Mr. Costigan.” He minds it. Then the second flight is long, and he has a story, and the comedy wins back half of her before the landing.

body: He tells her about Ocean Road, and he tells it for laughs, because it is one. La Flaca with no light. Rafi on his skateboard holding onto the basket and getting towed. A gray Crown Victoria coming up behind them slow as a hearse with a light going on the dash, and a man in a windbreaker leaning out the window: *License and registration.* To a bicycle. “And I gave it to him.” “You did *not*.” “My Ohio driver’s license. I handed it in the window.” Lena stops on the step and holds the rail. “He read it out loud. *John Anthony Costigan. Youngstown.*” And then Rafi coasting up out of the fog — *Pop.* The Vehicle Code by heart, a white lamp visible from three hundred feet. The bike reported abandoned at the harbor in 2007. *Your abuela is not a court.*

body.text: “And then I asked him if it was about the light or the bike.” “Oh, you *didn’t*.” “He said it was about my mouth.”
“I told him it was on me. No light. My fault.” “Of course you did,” she says, as if she’d have bet the house on it.
“I said, *Evening, Officer.*” “Oh, no.” “*Detective*,” Jack says, in the man’s voice, flat as a parking ticket.
“I put my hands on the bars and didn’t say a word. He told Rafi I know how to get pulled over. He said Rafi could learn.”

body: She laughs, properly, there on the stairs, her head down over the cold rail, and it comes back to them off the side of the lab. “What *is* he, Highway Patrol?”
“Rafi’s dad. Detective. Ochoa — like Rafi.”
Her hand goes to the medal at her collarbone. Two steps up, her thumb is still on the worn gold. “Was he kind to you?” she says. It’s a practical question, and she asks it like one.

“He gave me a light. Out of his trunk. *Found property*.” He tells her how the man got out and clipped it to the handlebar himself and clicked it on, white on the fog. “Good,” Lena says, and lets go of the medal.
On the next landing, under the caged bulb, she says, “On Monday you argued like he was in the room.” Not Ray. He knows who she means. “Did you ever find out what he was going to tell Gina?”
The letter is in his back pocket, folded in thirds against the Williams.

choices.text: Read her the line about Gina, and the one about her.
choices.key: You read Lena your brother’s letter: ‘Tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. I got it.’
response: Under the bulb he takes it out and unfolds it — lined paper, pencil, both sides — and finds the place. “*Tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. I got it.*” And lower down: “*Tell the veil girl thanks for asking my name. Nobody out there asks it anymore. They ask Ma how I’m doing like I’m the weather.*”

The pump hums behind the steel door. Then Lena says, “He sounds like somebody who’s used to carrying.” It’s kindly meant; he can hear that it is. Jack folds the letter back along its creases, thirds, and puts it away against the Williams. “Tell him he’s welcome,” she says.

choices.text: Tell her what he wrote about her. Keep Gina’s line.
choices.key: You told Lena your brother thanked her for asking his name.
response: He leaves the letter where it is. He has the line by heart already. “He says to tell the veil girl thanks for asking his name. *Nobody out there asks it anymore. They ask Ma how I’m doing like I’m the weather.*”
Lena is quiet up three steps. Then: “Tell him he’s welcome.”

choices.key: You kept Danny’s letter to yourself.
response: “Yeah,” he says. “He wrote.” And leaves it there.
She doesn’t push. A flight later she asks only, “You okay?” and he says, “Yeah,” and she takes it, for now. He can hear the *for now*.

s10c.slug: SUNDAY · 3:34 AM · THE LAGOON FOOTPATH, THE BENCH
body: The Lagoon smells like the bottom of a vase: salt and rot and something sweet under both. The footpath runs along the water on packed dirt, and out in the reeds something white moves and resettles and complains about it — an egret asleep on one leg, annoyed to be reminded. Across the water Delgado is a grid of dark windows with one or two still lit. Halfway along the path, under a pepper tree, there’s the bench. It faces the Lagoon. People have carved their initials into the back slat, and in a couple of places somebody has carved them out again.

Lena sits down on it. Jack sits at the other end. There’s a whole person’s worth of bench between them, and he keeps it. He wants to put his arm along the back slat. He wants a great deal more than that, plainly, and has since a porch in August, and he sits with his elbows on his knees and looks at the egret.
“Laney says this is where people come to break up,” Lena says.
“Are we breaking up?”
“We’d have to be something first, Costigan.”
She says it lightly. The egret settles. She’s already on to the next thing. “Have you read it? Tomorrow’s?”

He has. Mark nine. “Seventeen hours and twenty-six minutes,” Lena says, “not that anybody’s counting.” On the road the disciples argue about which of them is the greatest, and when they get to the house He asks them what they were arguing about on the way, and nobody says a word. “Because they were embarrassed,” Jack says. “Because they were *men*, Costigan. Twelve grown men, and not one of them would stand up and say, *Me, Lord. I said me.*” *If anyone wishes to be first, he shall be the last of all and the servant of all.*
“So who’s last this week?”

She holds up a finger. “Laney’s first. Laney has *sisters*.” “Becca’s kids are last,” Jack says. “All seven of them.” “Seven?” “Or nine. Odd numbers. So there’s a tiebreaker.” Lena puts her face in her hands. “Lord have mercy. She’s going to run a parish council out of a farmhouse.”
He looks at the water. “Danny’s last.”
The egret mutters in the reeds. Lena takes her face out of her hands and doesn’t make it into anything; she just says it, as though it’s posted on a sign by the door. “Then he’s first.”
He can’t leave that sitting there on the bench between them, so he gives her Rudy instead. “The dish man eats first. Soledad rule.”
“Then go eat something, dish man,” Lena says. “You look like a coat on a hanger.” And that’s the last word, and it’s hers.

At 3:52 Delgado’s basement laundry door is propped open with a folded *Marisol Tide*, RITES OF PASSAGE face up under Margot’s byline, the warm chemical sweetness of the dryers breathing out into the cold.

body.text: At the door he gives her back the boots. She takes them by the straps and holds them against her hip.

body: The elevator is down here by the vending machines, and it smells of detergent and somebody’s pizza. She presses 2. He presses 4. The doors close on the two of them and the car goes up, slow, the cables ticking, and neither of them looks at the other except in the scratched steel of the doors, which shows them anyway: a girl in a cardigan holding a pair of boots, a man with sand on his jeans, standing a careful foot apart.
At two the car stops. The doors open on the dark second-floor hall, the exit sign red at the far end of it. She steps out. Then she turns around.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately. She’s decided not to notice. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive.

choices.key: At the elevator you said, “Goodnight, Magdalena.” Twice now.
response: She holds the boots against her and looks at him from the hall. “That’s twice, Youngstown,” Lena says. “I keep a tin for less.” Then the doors come together on her — the cardigan, the boots, her face last, a line of light, gone — and the car goes on up to four with him in it.

“Goodnight, Jack,” she says. The doors slide shut between them, steel on steel, and the last of her he sees is a cardigan sleeve and a hand coming up, and then the car takes him the rest of the way up.
“Go to sleep, Costigan,” she says, smiling at the elevator buttons instead of at him. The doors close on the smile, and the car goes up with him and whatever’s left of it.

body: The Commons at 3:19 is a whole dark field with nobody on it. The sprinklers have been and gone; the lawn is soaked and cold and shines under the path lamps, and every step on it makes a small wet sound. Ferrer Tower stands over the middle of it, dark in the louvers, the clock face lit and every bell shut up for the night. It quit at ten. It won’t say a word till seven.
The RAZR goes off in his pocket. He tips the screen to the angle where it lights.

body.text: Asleep. On her side, per instructions. Breathing like a Vienna choirboy. Sloane has issued me a pillow shaped like a cowboy boot. —T.V.

body: He holds it out. Lena reads it and shuts her eyes for one step, then opens them, and walks on easier.
Halfway across, he asks the thing he’s wondered since August. “Why Marisol?”
“Money,” she says. “Notre Dame gave me half. Marisol gave me all of it.” Her hand finds the medal. “My daddy sells shrimp.” The hand comes down. “Why’d you?”
“You know why,” he says. “A.H.”
“*Come and say it to his face.*” She read his postcard on a porch in August, and she has it by heart.
“He said you were in his office Friday,” Jack says. “At two.”

She walks a few wet steps. “I went to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive.” That’s all. He waits for the rest of it across twenty yards of grass, and there isn’t any. Then she turns it, neatly: “How’s your nonna?”

response.text: “I answered her again,” he says. “Same jokes. Same order. She laughed in the same places.”
“I told her she’d asked,” he says. “I shouldn’t have.”
“I asked for my mother,” he says.

response: Lena doesn’t tell him she’s sorry. She walks beside him on the wet grass without saying anything. “My Mémère’s eighty-eight,” she says. “Breaux Bridge. Half the time now she calls me Claudine — that’s my daddy’s sister, who is sixty-one and sells State Farm in Lafayette — and I answer to it.” She shrugs inside the cardigan. “You answer to whatever name they’ve got left.”

response: Lena gives it real consideration, a hand on her chin, walking. “Tell her I’m considering it,” she says. “Tell her it depends on the pension.”
