response: Lena looks at him sidelong across the dark. “‘Good,’” she says. “You said that about your daddy once, in Malibu. I let you keep it.” They walk a little way on the grass. “I’m keeping a list now.”

s10w.slug: SUNDAY · 2:44 AM · CAMPUS POINT, THE LIFEGUARD TOWER
body: She turns it herself. She doesn’t look at him to do it.
“Wes missed eight-oh-four.”
The shutter knocks on its chain.

“My phone was in my tote in a barn with a mechanical bull in it, and at eight-oh-four it didn’t ring. Eight-thirty, nothing. Nine. I went out and stood by the mailbox on Seacliff like a war bride. At nine-forty it rang. From somewhere loud. Music, a lot of people, my brother Luc in the back yelling something about a cab. He said he loved me. Twice.” She picks at the hem of the cardigan. “Once for me, and I’m not sure who the other one was for.”
Out on the break a set comes through, three in a row, with nobody to ride them.
“He calls from somewhere loud a lot,” she says. “Lately.”
She pulls her knees up under the cardigan and sets her chin on them, and says it plainly, a thing decided before she ever sat down: “I’ve decided not to notice.”
The chain lets the shutter go, and catches it.

Jack has three things. He’s had them for weeks without knowing he was keeping them, and here they are, all three, in his mouth: a wall post liked from New Orleans in the dead middle of the night, a phone call from a party, a text in capitals from the Dome with the letters missing.

choices.text: “You don’t have to be fine with me.”
choices.key: When Lena said she’d decided not to notice, you told her she doesn’t have to be fine with you.
response: It’s his Ocean Road line, and she knows it the second it’s out; he watches her know it. “I know,” Lena says, chin on her knees. “That’s the problem, Youngstown.” Then, quieter: “If I stop being fine with you, I don’t know how I’m supposed to — ” She doesn’t finish. The shutter knocks, and that is the end of the sentence.

choices.key: You told Lena what you’ve noticed about Wes: the four a.m. like, the party call, the spelling.
response: So he tells her. Not much, and not dressed up. The first week of school, his wall post, liked from New Orleans at four in the morning Wes’s time. The night before the opener, at the Anchor, a call from a party at two in the morning Wes’s time — *He sounded happy*, she said. Last Sunday, from the Dome, the capitals and the missing letters. He lays the three things down on the boards between them and stops.

Lena is on her feet before he’s finished. “He was *sixteen*.” Her voice carries; there’s nobody out here to hear it but the tower. “His uncle’s boat. Aluminum, flat-bottomed, a motor you start with a rope. Four days. Gentilly, the edge of the Ninth Ward, people on roofs, people in attics with no water. He took my brother and my sister out a second-floor window next door — Jude and Josie, they were *nine* — one and then the other. He was sixteen years old.” She stands over him on the ramp with her arms wrapped around herself in the cardigan. “He’s a good man. Don’t.”
Then she sits back down, not close, and it’s worse, because it’s quiet. “You noticed,” she says. “Of course you noticed. You notice everything you’re not supposed to.”

choices.key: When Lena said she’d decided not to notice, you said okay, and let her.
response: “Okay,” he says.

She waits to see if there’s more, and there isn’t. The four in the morning and the two in the morning and the capitals go back down where he keeps things, and he keeps them. The shutter knocks. After a while she bumps his arm once with her shoulder, the knock of somebody in the next room letting you know they’re still in the house, and sits back.

choices.text: Make a joke about Luc’s spelling.
choices.key: You made a joke about Wes, and Lena asked you not to be funny. You stayed.
response: “Was Luc yelling in capitals too?”
It’s a good line. He can hear how good it is as it goes. Lena doesn’t laugh. She turns her face on her knees and looks at him, and her voice is very low. “Don’t. Don’t be funny right now. Just stay.”
So he stays. He sits on the ramp beside her with his hands between his knees while the shutter knocks and the break comes in pale out of the dark, and he says nothing at all, and he stays.

choices.text: Light a Red instead of answering.
choices.key: When Lena talked about Wes, you lit a cigarette instead of answering. She took it.
response: He doesn’t answer. He gets the Reds out of his back pocket, the pack crushed flat against the Williams, and lights one with his back to the wind. He gets exactly one drag. Lena reaches over without looking, takes it out of his mouth, puts it out in the sand beside the ramp, and has the Altoids tin out of her cardigan pocket and open before the smoke has cleared. She tears a strip off the bottom of a PI LAM RODEO flyer and writes on her knee by the light of her LG.

At ten past six the door opens and Theo comes in barefoot, with sand on his feet and the hems of his good jeans dark and wet to the shin, and hay still caught in the cashmere from the barn. He doesn’t turn the light on. He sits on the edge of his bed and starts picking straw off his sleeve one piece at a time.
“She woke up at four,” he says. Laney. “She asked for a waffle and her mother. Sloane produced a waffle.” He flicks a straw at the wastebasket and misses.

Theo looks at them in his palm. “Keep them for the Eagles.” “They’re your grandfather’s.” “He’d have liked the Eagles less.” Jack sets them on Theo’s nightstand anyway.

Lena is in the booth under it in her Keds, which means she’s happy, holding a coffee the size of a vase in both palms, on what she announces is three hours of sleep. Kevin is across from her in a 49ers cap with a basket of fries arranged by length. “I drove,” he says. “Designated adult. Also designated alarm clock. She answered the door in one shoe.” “I answered the door,” Lena says, “in a state of grace.”

body: At the end of the bar, Dale Wisniewski in the Barry Sanders jersey turns on his stool, sees Jack, and lifts his coffee an inch. “The loud one.” Last week Dale left a column of quarters and *next week, kid*. It’s next week. Jack lifts a hand back.

The Eagles have a kid at quarterback, first start, because McNabb’s ribs are cracked, and the kid is throwing it all over Philadelphia and throwing it, every so often, to the Saints. Midway through, the Eagles’ return man fumbles a kickoff, and two plays later the Saints are in the end zone, and the owner is on the brass bell with his whole shoulder, and Lena is standing on the booth seat with her coffee held out level so as not to lose any. “The kid’s going to be good,” Dale says of the Eagles quarterback. “You said that about the Lions kid,” Jack says. “I say it about all of them,” says Dale. “One of them’s going to be.”

She sits down. She tells Kevin she has been betrayed before God and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. Reggie Bush answers for it a few minutes later, nineteen yards untouched, and she stands back up and forgives everybody.

Final, forty-eight to twenty-two. Dale raps the table going out and leaves quarters. In the lot Lena wipes 1–0 off the Odyssey’s back glass with the hem of her cardigan, digs the La Vang car-wash polish out of her tote, and writes it big: 2–0. Kevin, keys out: “Still my mom’s car.” Lena caps the bottle and pats the glass like a horse. “Your mother’s car,” she says, “is undefeated.”

body: KESSLER SHOES is still ghosted in gold over the door, but under it the storefront has put on its Eid best: paper garlands in green and gold looped across the window, a hand-lettered EID MUBARAK taped to the glass, and inside, the wire shoe racks overflowing onto the sidewalk — men’s loafers, a pair of patent-leather Mary Janes, small sneakers that light up when a kid runs past them, which is constantly. Jack unlaces his boots. He checked his socks before he left Delgado. No holes. Yusuf, at the door, glances down at them anyway. “Progress,” he says.

He’s in a new kurta, pale gray with white thread at the collar, mailed from Fremont by his mother in a box that also contained, he reports, three pounds of dates and a letter about his hair. The folding tables along the back wall are buried: rice in foil pans, kebabs, bolani, a bowl of chickpeas the size of a birdbath, and a steel pot of sheer khurma, vermicelli in sweet milk with cardamom and dates and slivered pistachio, which a grandmother ladles into a paper cup and puts into Jack’s hands without asking his name. Kids in new clothes do laps between the tables. The uncle in the Raiders cap is here, in a better Raiders cap.
“Thirty days,” Yusuf says, loading a plate. “I can eat lunch.” He adds a second kebab. “I’m going to eat it twice.”

At twenty to one his phone goes, and his whole face changes before he’s even got it to his ear. He takes it out onto the sidewalk among the shoes. Through the window Jack watches him walk up and down past the laundromat in his socks, one hand flat on his head. He comes back in five minutes later, lighter by about a hundred pounds. “Tariq,” he says. “It’s ten past midnight there. It’s tomorrow.” He sits down. “He complained about the food. He’s fine.”

Over the second lunch, he explains zakat al-fitr, because Jack asks what the coffee can by the door with the slot in the lid is for. Before the Eid prayer, every household pays for food for the poor — so much per head, babies included. “You pay the poorest man’s breakfast before you’re allowed to pray for yours,” Yusuf says. “So nobody is hungry on the day.” He tears a piece of bolani in half and hands Jack the bigger piece, which Jack is beginning to understand is not an accident. “Load-bearing. You take it out, the feast falls down.”

body: Kevin is at the church door in the navy quarter-zip, handing out worship aids like a maître d’. “Browns lost, man,” he says, by way of hello. “Twenty-seven six.” He gives Jack a worship aid and a consoling squeeze of the shoulder, and Jack takes both.

The college Mass is standing room again: candles, the overheads off, the blue glass black, the hull of the ceiling going up into the dark over everybody. Three guitars and the cajón. Kenzie Rourke cantors the psalm — *The Lord upholds my life* — and her voice goes up into the ribs of the boat and hangs. Then Joey Abruzzo gets up to lector for the first time in his life and reads Wisdom at a volume that would carry across the Staten Island Ferry in a gale. *Let us see whether his words be true.* In the second pew Kevin sits forward with his elbows on his knees, and his lips are moving along with every word; Joey’s been coached. Then James, and one line out of it Jack hears and keeps: *You covet but do not possess.*
Then Mark. The road through Galilee, and the Twelve behind Him, arguing.

Osei preaches from the step with the reading glasses on their cord. “On the road they argued about who was the greatest,” he says. “In the house He asked them what they had been talking about, and they were silent.” He looks out at them over the glasses. “Every one of us has been silent in that house.” And he sits.

Laney is between them. She came in at 8:58 hungover and pink, in her new Pi Lam letters under Lena’s oatmeal cardigan, sunglasses pushed up into the copper hair, and sat down in the middle without discussing it, and now she sits through the Eucharistic Prayer with her eyes shut and her hands folded like she’s seen it done. At the Our Father she takes Lena’s hand and squeezes it, and doesn’t let go of it after the Amen.

At the sign of peace she turns to Lena first. “I’m sorry I called you a mother.” Lena looks at her, at the sunglasses and the letters and the cardigan, which is hers. “Cher,” she says. “Somebody has to be.” Then Laney turns and shakes Jack’s hand with both of hers and great dignity, and over the top of her head Lena gives him her hand, too.

body: At Communion Laney goes up between them with her arms crossed over the Pi Lam letters for the blessing, the way she did at her first, like a Baptist, and comes back with her eyes down and her mouth closed tight on something that isn’t a joke.

During the recessional Becca Lindell turns around, two rows up across the aisle — she did it at the peace, too — and waves at him with her whole hand, the whole arm going, a rancher’s wave across a pasture.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Shadowed in an ER this summer. Tells his mother he’s asleep. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Coached Joey through his first reading and mouthed every word of it from the second pew.

response: He lifts a hand and waves back, a real wave, and Becca beams like he’s answered something. She points at him over the heads of the people filing out and mouths a word across the aisle. It’s probably *Friday*. The question mark is still on her face when the crowd takes her out the door.
Beside him Lena is very busy finding the sleeve of her own cardigan on Laney.

choices.text: Tell Laney she did beautifully, in Lena’s bulletin voice.
response: He leans down to her ear and gives it the full parish bulletin, the voice of a note written on the back of one: “You are doing beautifully.” Laney goes pink to the hairline. “Sugar,” she says, “I *know*.”
On her other side, Lena keeps her eyes on the recessional and pretends she didn’t hear a word of it. The corner of her mouth gives her away.

He stays down on the kneeler while the church empties around him, hoodies and backpacks, the candles guttering in the draft from the doors. The last guitar chord rings in the hull and quits. He prays the way he always has, short and plain, to Someone in the next room: *Nonna. Danny. Gina. Her. Me, if there’s any left over.*
When he gets up and goes out, Lena and Laney are under the olive tree in the dark, Laney’s head on Lena’s shoulder, waiting for him.

He addresses the envelope in block capitals from memory — the name, the number, the institution, the town — and presses hard enough that the letters stand up on the back. The RAZR lies open on the desk beside it with the screen dark. There’s nothing from her tonight, and the phone can stay dark.

He folds the letter in three, along the lines, and runs his thumbnail down each crease. Across the room the clip starts over, arms wide, silent, and Theo breathes in, slow, and out, slow, and keeps on doing it.
